cross_exam_prompt_render.why: harness-log: CROSS_EXAM_PROMPT contains a JSON output template, so str.format() treats its { } as placeholders and raises KeyError. Rendering was extracted into build_cross_exam_message() and must keep using str.replace().

mutations.desc: Re-inject the original defect: render with str.format(colleagues=...) instead of str.replace().
Inline the rendering back into cross_examine(), leaving build_cross_exam_message() as dead code. The behavioural tests stay green; only the structural test can catch this divergence.

stdout_gbk_guard.why: P4: when stdout is redirected, Python falls back to the local code page (GBK / cp936), so printing a character GBK cannot encode raises UnicodeEncodeError and throws away the whole output plus the exit code. The correct guard -- measured, not reasoned -- is reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"); both keywords are required.

mutations.desc: Guard sys.stderr instead of sys.stdout: the guard is textually present and looks right, but stdout still crashes.

Drop encoding="utf-8", keeping only errors="replace". Nothing crashes any more, but the output stays GBK bytes and is unreadable to anything that reads UTF-8. This is exactly the mistake the author made first.
Call reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", errors="strict"): strict IS the default, so the error mode is exactly equivalent to having no guard at all -- yet it looks identical to the real thing.

chat_call_signature.why: A call site passed max_tokens=2048 to DeepSeekClient.chat(), whose signature has no such parameter. No unit test could reach it (the adjudication step costs real API calls), so it only exploded after the whole multi-agent loop had run and the money was already spent. The seal is a static check that every chat() call site matches the real signature.

mutations.desc: Re-inject the historical defect: pass max_tokens=2048 to chat() inside adjudicate().
mutations.replace:
tools=None,          # 协调者不查数据 —— 它只裁决
        tag="coordinator",
        max_tokens=2048,
    )

mutations.desc: Inject a bogus kwarg at the call site in specialist.py instead. If the check only looked at coordinator.py, this mutant would stay green.

scoring_and_reproducibility.why: Three separate ways the D7 measurement lied: (#16) the keyword scorer counted a mention that the answer explicitly DISMISSED, so the multi-agent run was scored 100% while it had actually fallen for the red herring; (#17) the cross-examination step budget was hardcoded to 4 and not wired to --max-steps, while the report told the user to raise --max-steps; (#18) CrossExam snapshots omitted `finished`, so a 'convergence 0%' report could not say which role failed; (#19) root_cause was truncated to 400 chars while `correct` was computed on the full text, so 2 of 18 stored verdicts could not be reproduced from their own archive.

mutations.desc: #16: remove the dismissal check, so a keyword counts even when the answer explicitly rejects it. This is exactly how the red-herring verdict was scored 100%.
mutations.find:
if any(m in clause for m in DISMISSAL_MARKERS):
                    continue

mutations.desc: #16 follow-up: split only on sentence punctuation, not on commas. Then 'the root cause is NOT the pool, but the slow risk service' is read as one sentence containing a negation, and a CORRECT answer gets marked wrong. Guards against over-correcting into false negatives.
#17: give cross_examine a default step budget again (4, as it was). A default lets a caller spend a budget nobody measured without deciding anything.
#17: keep the CLI flag but stop passing it down. A parameter that exists, can be set, and has no effect is equivalent to the original defect.

#19: truncate root_cause to 400 chars again while `correct` keeps being computed on the full text -- the stored evidence then cannot reproduce its own verdict.

#19, other layer: truncate inside Attempt.to_dict() instead -- the plausible version of this mistake ('results.json is getting big, let's trim it'). Guards the save/load round-trip invariant, which the slice-level test does not cover.

fault_catalog_integrity.why: A fault definition carries two hand-written lists: `patches` (what really changes) and `changes` (what gets written to the change log). Their only link is an env-var name, so a mismatch is silent: the scenario still runs and still writes data, but the change record comes out as `from: null, to: null`. That is corrupted data, not a harder scenario -- and it only shows up when a NEW fault is added, which is exactly when nobody is looking.

mutations.desc: Restore the historical bug: map env-var names through a short hand-maintained dict with an env_key.lower() fallback. Then any newly added fault silently writes null change values.
Drop the pool_size -> pool_limit alias, so F2's change key stops resolving. Shows the self-check covers aliased names too, not just derived ones.

#20: make the F7 precondition guard a no-op. F7's whole value is that the recorded change is causally irrelevant, which only holds while concurrency < pool capacity. A guard that no longer guards turns F7 back into F2's mistake.

invalidated_scenario_exclusion.why: #20: F2's ground truth was proven inverted by a control experiment, but the scenario is kept in the catalog as a documented counter-example. That creates a new risk -- the bad question keeps polluting every accuracy comparison, invisibly (you just think 'accuracy is low'). Excluding it must be a mechanism (a field + filtering in the aggregate + disclosure in the report), not a matter of remembering.

mutations.desc: Stop filtering invalidated scenarios out of the aggregate -- the historical behaviour, where a wrong question silently drags every number down.
mutations.find: scored = [a for a in self.attempts if a.fault_id not in invalidated]

mutations.desc: Keep excluding invalidated scenarios but stop reporting them. Then the reader believes every scenario was counted -- 'the number looks fine, but it is not measuring what you think'.
